slot.brief: Car on a banked curve with no friction; ask for the optimum speed given banking angle and radius, using tan θ = v²/(rg).

stem: A curved road of radius $120$ m is banked at an angle $\theta$ such that $\sin\theta = 0.6$. What is the speed at which a car can take this curve safely without relying on friction? (Take $g = 10$ m s$^{-2}$.)

verdicts.working:
Given $\sin\theta = 0.6$, we have $\tan\theta = \frac{0.6}{0.8} = 0.75$.
The optimum banking speed without friction is $v = \sqrt{R g \tan\theta} = \sqrt{120 \times 10 \times 0.75} = \sqrt{900} = 30\text{ m s}^{-1}$.
Converting to $\text{km h}^{-1}$: $v = 30 \times \frac{18}{5} = 108\text{ km h}^{-1}$.

working:
With no friction, the horizontal component of the normal reaction supplies the centripetal force, and the vertical component balances the weight:
$$N\sin\theta = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}, \qquad N\cos\theta = mg \;\Rightarrow\; \tan\theta = \dfrac{v^2}{rg}.$$
Since $\sin\theta = 0.6$, we have $\cos\theta = 0.8$ and $\tan\theta = \dfrac{3}{4}$.
$$v^2 = rg\tan\theta = 120 \times 10 \times \dfrac{3}{4} = 900 \;\Rightarrow\; v = 30\ \text{m s}^{-1}.$$
Converting to km h$^{-1}$: $30 \times \dfrac{18}{5} = 108$ km h$^{-1}$.
